expansion:
Corneal ulcer is the keyed cause of photophobia because the lecture lists it as a direct symptom of bacterial keratitis (which produces a corneal ulcer): “Bacterial Keratitis: Clinical Features & Investigations... Symptoms: Pain, photophobia, blurred vision, mucopurulent discharge – acute onset” (L15,16, page 9). The cornea is densely innervated, and an epithelial defect with underlying stromal inflammation irritates these nerve endings and triggers reflex ciliary spasm, which is experienced as an abnormal sensitivity to light. The companion Red Eye lecture makes the same mechanism explicit for corneal/anterior-segment inflammation generally: “Photophobia is an abnormal sensitivity to light that accompanies iridocyclitis, either alone or secondary to corneal inflammation. Patients with conjunctivitis have normal light sensitivity” (L37) Red Eye.txt).

Immature senile cataract, option A, is a lens opacity that reduces and blurs vision through light scatter, but the lens has no sensory innervation of its own and a cataract does not irritate corneal nerves or provoke ciliary spasm, so it is not a recognised cause of photophobia (not taken from the course material).

Retinal detachment, option C, is a posterior-segment disease affecting the neurosensory retina; it can cause photopsia (flashes of light) and field loss, but it does not inflame or irritate the richly innervated anterior structures (cornea, iris, ciliary body) that generate the photophobia response, so it is not a cause of true photophobia (not taken from the course material).

Senile macular degeneration, option D, affects the central retina at the macula and causes distorted or reduced central vision; like retinal detachment, it is a posterior-segment process with no effect on corneal or iridociliary innervation, and it is not listed among photophobia-producing conditions (not taken from the course material).
objective: Identify corneal ulcer (via bacterial keratitis) as a cause of photophobia, as distinct from posterior-segment and lens conditions that do not irritate anterior-segment nerves
